claim: Biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation dynamically exchange material with their surroundings.
source: A hallmark of biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation is that they dynamically exchange material with their surroundings, and this process can be crucial to condensate function.
evidence: This is stated as a hallmark property in the abstract, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Material exchange can be crucial to condensate function.
source: A hallmark of biomolecular condensates formed via liquid-liquid phase separation is that they dynamically exchange material with their surroundings, and this process can be crucial to condensate function.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the abstract.

claim: The rate of exchange can be limited by the flux from the dilute phase.
source: Intuitively, the rate of exchange can be limited by the flux from the dilute phase or by the mixing speed in the dense phase.
evidence: This is presented as an intuitive understanding in the abstract.

claim: The rate of exchange can be limited by the mixing speed in the dense phase.
source: Intuitively, the rate of exchange can be limited by the flux from the dilute phase or by the mixing speed in the dense phase.
evidence: This is presented as an intuitive understanding in the abstract.

claim: A recent experiment suggests that exchange can be limited by the dynamics at the droplet interface.
source: Surprisingly, a recent experiment suggests that exchange can also be limited by the dynamics at the droplet interface, implying the existence of an 'interface resistance'.
evidence: This references experimental findings from Taylor et al., 2019 as discussed later in the manuscript.

claim: Interface resistance can arise when incident molecules transiently touch the interface without entering the dense phase.
source: We then utilize sticker-spacer polymer models to show that interface resistance can arise when incident molecules transiently touch the interface without entering the dense phase, i.e., the molecules 'bounce' from the interface.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' modeling work presented in the manuscript.

claim: Biomolecular condensates organize the interior of cells in both space and time.
source: The interior of cells is organized in both space and time by biomolecular condensates, which form and dissolve as needed (Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Biomolecular condensates form and dissolve as needed.
source: The interior of cells is organized in both space and time by biomolecular condensates, which form and dissolve as needed (Shin and Brangwynne, 2017; Banani et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior work.

claim: Condensates play key roles in processes ranging from transcription to translation, metabolism, signaling, and more.
source: These condensates play key roles in processes ranging from transcription to translation, metabolism, signaling, and more (An et al., 2008; Su et al., 2016; Sabari et al., 2018; Formicola et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior work.

claim: Complex interactions among condensate components endow condensates with distinct physical properties including low surface tension, viscoelasticity, and aging.
source: The complex interactions among their components endow condensates with distinct physical properties, including low surface tension, viscoelasticity, aging, etc.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about condensate properties.

claim: The rate of exchange can impact biochemical processes by limiting the escape of completed products.
source: This rate of exchange can impact biochemical processes taking place in condensates by limiting the escape of completed products (e.g. ribosomes produced in nucleoli; Yao et al., 2019), or limiting the availability of components or regulatory molecules (e.g. snoRNAs and ribosomal proteins entering nucleoli, or mRNAs entering P bodies or stress granules).
evidence: This is supported by a citation and specific examples.

claim: The rate of exchange can limit the availability of components or regulatory molecules in condensates.
source: This rate of exchange can impact biochemical processes taking place in condensates by limiting the escape of completed products (e.g. ribosomes produced in nucleoli; Yao et al., 2019), or limiting the availability of components or regulatory molecules (e.g. snoRNAs and ribosomal proteins entering nucleoli, or mRNAs entering P bodies or stress granules).
evidence: This is stated with specific examples of biological systems.

claim: The rate of exchange can control the dynamical response of condensates to a changing environment.
source: The rate of exchange can also control the dynamical response of condensates to a changing environment, and, as exchange between dense and dilute phase is central to coarsening via Ostwald ripening, it can regulate the number, size, and location of condensates within the cell.
evidence: This is stated as a logical consequence of exchange dynamics.

claim: Exchange between dense and dilute phase is central to coarsening via Ostwald ripening.
source: The rate of exchange can also control the dynamical response of condensates to a changing environment, and, as exchange between dense and dilute phase is central to coarsening via Ostwald ripening, it can regulate the number, size, and location of condensates within the cell.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about phase separation physics.

claim: Material exchange can be probed via FRAP experiments.
source: The material exchange between a condensate and the surrounding dilute phase can be probed via FRAP experiments, a commonly used approach for measuring condensate fluidity and molecular diffusion coefficients.
evidence: This is stated as a commonly used experimental approach.

claim: Exchange dynamics have been reported for a variety of systems.
source: Exchange dynamics are thus readily measurable and have been reported for a variety of systems (Li et al., 2012; Patel et al., 2015; Burke et al., 2015; Banani et al., 2016; Jain et al., 2016; Aumiller et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior experimental work.

claim: Only a very limited number of studies aimed to understand what controls the timescales of condensate component exchange.
source: However, only a very limited number of studies (Taylor et al., 2019; Hubatsch et al., 2021; Bo et al., 2021; Folkmann et al., 2021; Lee, 2021) aimed to understand what controls the timescales of condensate component exchange.
evidence: This is stated with specific citations to the limited prior work.

claim: Taylor et al., 2019 combined FRAP experiments on condensates in vitro and in vivo with different theoretical models to examine the impact of model choice on physical parameters derived from data fitting.
source: Briefly, Taylor et al., 2019 combined FRAP experiments on condensates in vitro and in vivo with different theoretical models to examine the impact of model choice on the physical parameters derived from data fitting (Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This describes the approach of a cited study.

claim: Folkmann et al., 2021 and Lee, 2021 proposed that the rate of molecular absorption to the condensate can be 'conversion-limited' instead of diffusion-limited.
source: Folkmann et al., 2021 and Lee, 2021 proposed that the rate of molecular absorption to the condensate can be 'conversion-limited' instead of diffusion-limited and established a mathematical framework for the temporal evolution of droplet sizes in this limit (Folkmann et al., 2021; Lee, 2021).
evidence: This describes findings from cited studies.

claim: The modeling of interface resistance in prior studies was conducted at the phenomenological level without aiming to understand the underlying physical mechanism.
source: In all these cases, the modeling of interface resistance (Taylor et al., 2019) or conversion-limited material transfer (Folkmann et al., 2021; Lee, 2021) was conducted at the phenomenological level, without aiming to understand the underlying physical mechanism that gives rise to interface resistance.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work by the authors.

claim: Mean-field approaches in Hubatsch et al., 2021 and Bo et al., 2021 neglect the potentially complex dynamics of molecules at the condensate interface.
source: However, the mean-field approaches in Hubatsch et al., 2021 and Bo et al., 2021 neglect the potentially complex dynamics of molecules at the condensate interface, which can slow down material exchange significantly as suggested by Taylor et al., 2019 and Folkmann et al., 2021.
evidence: This is a critical assessment of prior work supported by citations.

claim: A large interface resistance was proposed as a possible explanation for the discrepancy between measured and predicted LAF-1 recovery times.
source: A large interface resistance was proposed as a possible explanation for this discrepancy (Taylor et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from a cited study.

claim: The existence of a large interface resistance necessarily implies a strongly reduced flux of molecules successfully crossing the interface.
source: The existence of a large interface resistance then necessarily implies a strongly reduced flux of molecules successfully crossing the interface.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the definition of interface resistance.

claim: Bouncing can occur because molecules incident from the dilute phase fail to incorporate into the interface, or they transiently incorporate but fail to enter the dense phase.
source: This can occur either because the molecules incident from the dilute phase fail to incorporate into the interface, or they transiently incorporate but fail to enter the dense phase. In both cases, the molecules effectively 'bounce' from the interface leading to a large interface resistance.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The 'sticker-spacer' model provides a conceptual framework for understanding biomolecular phase separation.
source: The 'sticker-spacer' model provides a conceptual framework for understanding biomolecular phase separation, wherein the 'stickers' represent residues or larger domains that are capable of forming saturable bonds, while the 'spacers' connect the stickers to form polymers.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the sticker-spacer model.

claim: Polymers like A6B6 with long blocks of stickers of the same type have low dilute-phase concentrations.
source: As found previously (Weiner et al., 2021), polymers like A6B6 with long blocks of stickers of the same type have low dilute-phase concentrations.
evidence: This is supported by a citation and confirmed by the authors' simulations.

claim: Long-block polymers have low dense-phase diffusion coefficients because of their large number of trans-bonds.
source: These long-block polymers also have low dense-phase diffusion coefficients because of their large number of trans-bonds, which need to be repeatedly broken for the polymers to diffuse.
evidence: This is an inference from simulation results with physical reasoning.

claim: The reduction in interface conductance can be traced to a 'bouncing' effect where molecules incident from the dilute phase fail to form bonds with the dense phase.
source: This reduction can be traced to a 'bouncing' effect. As shown schematically in the inset to Figure 3D and for an exemplary simulated trajectory in Figure 3E (more trajectories can be found in Appendix 2), molecules incident from the dilute phase may fail to form bonds with the dense phase, effectively 'bouncing' off of the condensate.
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' simulations with visual evidence in Figure 3D and 3E.

claim: The interface conductance of sticker-spacer polymers is controlled by the encounter rate of a pair of unbound stickers and the availability of these stickers.
source: More generally, we find that the interface conductance of the sticker-spacer polymers is controlled by the encounter rate of a pair of unbound stickers and the availability of these stickers, which in turn depends on the sticker-sticker binding strength, the dilute- and dense-phase polymer concentrations, and the width of the interface:
evidence: This is a finding from the authors' analysis of simulation results.

claim: At equal stoichiometry, both free As and free Bs are rare which maximizes the bouncing effect.
source: By contrast, at equal stoichiometry, both free As and free Bs are rare which maximizes the bouncing effect.
evidence: This is an inference from simulation results with mechanistic reasoning.

claim: The reduction in potential binding partners at equal stoichiometry causes an anomalous slowing of diffusion within condensates in the regime of strong binding.
source: This reduction in potential binding partners at equal stoichiometry has also been observed experimentally (Brassinne et al., 2017), and theoretically Ronceray et al., 2022, to cause an anomalous slowing of diffusion within condensates at equal stoichiometry in the regime of strong binding.
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental and theoretical work.

claim: The FRAP recovery curve obtained from simulation agrees almost perfectly with the numerical integration of the theoretical model.
source: The resulting numerical curve agrees almost perfectly with the simulation result (Figure 4D), which validates both our theoretical and simulation approaches.
evidence: This is a validation result shown in Figure 4D comparing simulation and theory.

claim: The FRAP recovery of the simulated droplet is clearly limited by the interface resistance.
source: The FRAP recovery of the simulated droplet is clearly limited by the interface resistance.
evidence: This is an inference from comparing the measured recovery time to theoretical predictions shown in Figure 5A.

claim: For small droplets, interface resistance dominates recovery times, whereas for large droplets, dense-phase diffusion dominates recovery times.
source: The interface resistance dominates recovery times for smaller droplets, whereas dense-phase diffusion dominates recovery times for larger droplets.
evidence: This is shown in Figure 5A caption and the figure itself.

claim: For large droplets, progressive diffusion of fluorescence into the droplet will be apparent, whereas small droplets will recover uniformly.
source: In the latter case, the fluorescence profile during recovery will be notably different in large versus small droplets as shown in Figure 5B – for large droplets progressive diffusion of fluorescence into the droplet will be apparent, whereas small droplets will recover uniformly as internal mixing will be fast compared to exchange with the surroundings.
evidence: This is a prediction from the theoretical model illustrated in Figure 5B.

claim: The dynamic exchange of condensate components with the surroundings is a key feature of membraneless organelles.
source: The dynamic exchange of condensate components with the surroundings is a key feature of membraneless organelles, and can significantly impact condensate biological function.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: The essential requirement for bouncing is that molecules in the dilute phase and molecules at the interface should not present 'sticky' surfaces to each other.
source: The essential requirement is that molecules in the dilute phase and molecules at the interface should not present 'sticky' surfaces to each other.
evidence: This is a mechanistic principle inferred from the simulation results.

claim: A natural scenario for bouncing is that molecules assume non-sticky conformations due to the shielding of interacting regions.
source: Since these same molecules must be capable of sticking to each other in order to phase separate, a natural scenario is that these molecules assume non-sticky conformations due to the shielding of interacting regions, e.g., burial of hydrophobic residues in the core of a protein, or, in the scenario explored in the simulations, the saturation of sticker-like bonds.
evidence: This is a mechanistic hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Examples of systems with strong enough bonds to allow bond saturation include SIM-SUMO and nucleic acids with strong intramolecular base-pairing.
source: Examples of systems with strong enough bonds to allow bond saturation include SIM-SUMO (Banani et al., 2016) and nucleic acids with strong intramolecular base-pairing.
evidence: This is stated with a citation to support one example.

claim: A coarse-grained simulation of RNA droplets of (CAG)47 illustrated that a molecule in a closed hairpin conformation fails to integrate into a droplet but rather bounces off the droplet interface.
source: Interestingly, a recent coarse-grained simulation of RNA droplets of (CAG)47 (Nguyen et al., 2022) illustrated that a (CAG)47 molecule in a closed hairpin conformation fails to integrate into a droplet but rather bounces off the droplet interface.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited simulation study.

claim: Charged molecules could arrange themselves to form a charged layer at the interface, resulting in a high energetic barrier from electrostatic repulsion.
source: Another possible scenario is that charged molecules could arrange themselves to form a charged layer at the interface, resulting in a high energetic barrier from electrostatic repulsion for a dilute-phase component to reach and cross the interface (Ray et al., 2023; Dai et al., 2023; Majee et al., 2024).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to recent work.

claim: Ddx4-YFP droplets in the cell nucleus exhibit negligible interface resistance.
source: It has been shown that Ddx4-YFP droplets in the cell nucleus exhibit negligible interface resistance (Taylor et al., 2019), which raises the question whether interface resistance is relevant to natural condensates in vivo.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited experimental study.

claim: Formation of multiple layers or the presence of excess molecules of one species coating the droplet is likely to increase interface resistance.
source: Interestingly, formation of multiple layers or the presence of excess molecules of one species coating the droplet is likely to increase interface resistance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: The Pickering effect involves adsorbed particles partially covering the interface, thereby reducing the accessible area and the overall condensate surface tension, slowing down the exchange dynamics.
source: A notable example is the Pickering effect, in which adsorbed particles partially cover the interface, thereby reducing the accessible area and the overall condensate surface tension, slowing down the exchange dynamics (Folkmann et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a mechanism described with a citation.

claim: The same interface resistance that governs exchange between phases at equilibrium will control the flux of material from the dilute phase to the dense phase during coarsening.
source: The same interface resistance that governs exchange between phases at equilibrium will control the flux of material from the dilute phase to the dense phase during coarsening, so that bouncing will slow down the coarsening process.
evidence: This is a logical inference about the implications of interface resistance.

claim: A theoretical study of coarsening via mergers of small polymer clusters found anomalously slow coarsening dynamics due to exhaustion of binding sites.
source: Indeed, a recent theoretical study (Ranganathan and Shakhnovich, 2020) of coarsening via mergers of small polymer clusters found anomalously slow coarsening dynamics due to exhaustion of binding sites, paralleling the single-polymer bouncing effect explored here.
evidence: This is a finding from a cited theoretical study.

claim: A conversion-limited flux has been shown to lead to qualitatively distinct scaling of condensate size with time.
source: Interestingly, a conversion-limited flux has been shown to lead to qualitatively distinct scaling of condensate size with time (Lee, 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from a cited study.

claim: Many condensates dissolve and reform every cell cycle.
source: As many condensates dissolve and reform every cell cycle (or as needed), we anticipate that interfacial exchange will constitute an additional means of regulating condensate dynamics.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about condensate behavior.

claim: Interfacial exchange will constitute an additional means of regulating condensate dynamics.
source: As many condensates dissolve and reform every cell cycle (or as needed), we anticipate that interfacial exchange will constitute an additional means of regulating condensate dynamics.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors.

claim: Individual polymers are modeled as linear chains of spherical stickers of types A and B connected by implicit spacers.
source: Individual polymers are modeled as linear chains of spherical stickers of types A and B connected by implicit spacers (Figure 2A) with the interaction potentials in Equations 9–11, which ensure one-to-one binding between A and B stickers.
evidence: This describes the simulation methodology used by the authors.

claim: The system has reached equilibrium as indicated by consistency of results across replicates and across the first and second halves of the recorded data.
source: Consistency of results is checked across replicates and across the first and second halves of the recorded data. The agreement indicates that the system has reached equilibrium.
evidence: This is a validation of the simulation methodology.
